#9728. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

#9727. Survival Under the Allowlist: A Sharded, Agent-Assisted Design for Censorship-Resistant Networks

Independent researcher & technical writer exploring video games, blockchain, decentralized systems, and emerging technologies.

Independent researcher & technical writer exploring video games, blockchain, decentralized systems, and emerging technologies.

Independent researcher & technical writer exploring video games, blockchain, decentralized systems, and emerging technologies.

How internet control moved from blocklists to allowlists, why today's circumvention tools struggle with that shift, and a design sketch that combines local AI agents, sharded relay discovery, and a thin web3 coordination layer.

For a long time, the mental model of internet censorship was a blocklist. An authority decided that certain domains, IP addresses, or keywords were forbidden, and the network enforced it. Everything else worked. Circumvention was a race: find a path the list did not cover.

That model is eroding. In 2025 and 2026, several things happened at once:

This article does two things. First, it gives a unified technical picture of how modern network control works, drawing on published measurement research and reporting, so that readers who are not specialists in this field can see the whole system. Second, it proposes a design direction, built from existing research, that tries to answer a specific question: what would a circumvention network look like if it assumed that allowlists, per-ISP differences, and AI-assisted blocking are the normal case?

A note on scope. Iran, China, Russia, and North Korea are used here as points on a spectrum rather than as targets of an indictment. Iran is a particularly instructive hybrid, because its infrastructure draws on both Chinese and Russian technology (more on that below). The focus is technical: how the systems work, where current tools fail, and what might do better.

Nothing in this article is a finished invention. Most building blocks come from published research. The contribution, if there is one, is the composition, and an honest list of what remains unsolved.

This design also sits in the decentralized-AI stack. The agent runs small models on the user’s device (edge inference) rather than calling a central inference API, route intelligence is shared through a ledger with no single operator, and the aim is an AI-assisted network that is hard for any single party to switch off.

The shift can be summarized in four overlapping eras. This is a simplification, since all four coexist in different places, but it is a useful frame.

DNS poisoning, IP blocking, HTTP blockpages

OONI's 2014–2017 Iran measurements found DNS injection and transparent proxies serving blockpages, with circumvention-tool sites themselves blocked and Tor blocked on many networks

Inspect traffic and block what looks suspicious

Protocol fingerprinting, SNI inspection, active probing

The Great Firewall's passive detection of fully encrypted traffic (first reported in November 2021); SNI-based QUIC blocking from April 2024; Russia's TSPU boxes

Blocked-by-default networks, approved-user tiers, whitelisted IP ranges

Russian mobile whitelists (2025); Iran's tiered access during the 2026 shutdowns

A domestic network is the default; the global internet is exceptional

North Korea's intranet model; analysts describe Iran's trajectory as a new stage of digital isolation

The key observation is that each era is harder to circumvent than the last, for a different reason. Era 2 breaks tools that rely on looking like something else. Era 3 breaks tools that rely on being reachable at all, unless they can hide inside the allowed set.

A useful way to understand what a censor can see and do is to go layer by layer.

Reaching specific servers, or entire address families

Handshake metadata (TLS SNI, QUIC initial packets)

The destination name in the first packets

Reaching specific sites even when content is encrypted

Protocol fingerprints, packet sizes and timing, entropy-like heuristics

Known VPN and proxy protocols, and some unknown ones

The censor connects to suspected proxies and tests them

Only specific protocols or ports permitted

Differential pricing or quotas by destination

Two examples show how these layers interact.

The Great Firewall (GFW) is the reference system. Research from Wu et al. (USENIX Security 2023) found that in early November 2021 the GFW deployed a technique that passively detects fully encrypted traffic, such as that produced by Shadowsocks, VMess, and obfs4. Rather than defining what fully encrypted traffic is, the censor applies crude heuristics (protocol fingerprints, the fraction of set bits, and the number and position of printable ASCII characters) to exempt traffic that is unlikely to be fully encrypted, then blocks the rest. The authors estimated that such rules could block roughly 0.6 percent of normal traffic as collateral damage. A key finding is that randomness itself became a signal. The study's artifact repository also records that the GFW had stopped this dynamic blocking at least since 15 March 2023, a reminder that these systems change on their own schedule.

In 2024 the GFW began another capability. Zohaib et al. (USENIX Security 2025) report that since 7 April 2024 it blocks QUIC connections to specific domains, even though QUIC handshakes are encrypted, by decrypting QUIC initial packets at scale. The Register's summary notes the system cannot block all QUIC traffic and that its success rate fluctuates by time of day, and UMass researchers explain that the computational burden of inspecting those packets can overwhelm the system under modest load. The lesson for designers is that censors have capacity limits and collateral costs. (Such limits are not an invitation to attack national infrastructure: doing so would also harm ordinary users.)

Russia's approach is built on a different architecture. A 2019 law required operators to install DPI equipment. Measurement research on TSPU (IMC 2022) found that the boxes are deployed close to users while remaining centrally controlled. An earlier NDSS 2020 study found significant differences in the type and amount of blocking between ISPs.

Since then, the system has moved toward allowlisting. Global Voices describes whitelists applied during mobile shutdowns in 2025, and the Moscow Times quoted a ministry source describing shutdowns in Moscow as a test of the ability to block sites not on the whitelist.

Iran's system combines elements of both. A FOCI 2020 study documented a protocol whitelister that permitted only a small set of protocols (DNS, HTTP, HTTPS). More recent measurement work, IRBlock (USENIX Security 2025), finds that Iran's blocking strategies resemble the GFW's in many respects. A 2025 preprint describes a "stealth blackout" in which global routing appeared intact while users were isolated through DPI and protocol-based filtering, which is exactly the pattern that makes outage dashboards misleading.

The January 2026 shutdown is documented in unusual technical detail. FilterWatch's report, built on IODA, Kentik, and Cloudflare Radar data, describes a phased operation. In the days before 8 January, interference showed up as "zombie connections": devices looked connected at the IP layer while higher-layer performance was sabotaged, and VPNs showed "connected" but passed no data. On 8 January, 98.5 percent of Iranian IPv6 address space was withdrawn hours before the full cut, which the report interprets as herding traffic onto IPv4 infrastructure where inspection tools are more mature. Connectivity then fell to under 1 percent of normal. Restoration followed a blocked-by-default pattern in which services such as Google Search returned while the wider internet stayed dark, and, as an Iranian digital-rights researcher told Global Voices, whitelisting was enforced at the infrastructure level and not only at the service level. Its February 28 investigation describes "white" SIM cards and tiered pricing for international traffic. Iran International describes a related scheme branded "Internet Pro," in which access is organized around approved users and services.

Censorship infrastructure is increasingly a commercial product. In September 2025, more than 500 GB of source code, work logs, and internal documents from Geedge Networks and a related Chinese Academy of Sciences lab leaked. Tom's Hardware and the Jamestown Foundation describe deployments in Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar, and Kazakhstan, as well as Chinese provinces such as Xinjiang and Fujian. The data suggest that a censorship system can now be bought, configured, and operated by an ISP without building it from scratch.

Iran shows the same thing from the other side. ARTICLE 19 documents Chinese support for Iran's infrastructure over more than a decade, including equipment from ZTE, Huawei, Tiandy, and Hikvision. On the Russian side, Global Voices recounts Citizen Lab's 2023 finding that Protei, a company with Russian roots, was selected to provide core network components, including DPI, to the Iranian mobile operator Ariantel, and notes Foreign Policy's reporting of Russian help in building Iran's control architecture. The same article is explicit that it remains unclear exactly what Protei supplied.

For designers, the implication is simple: the problem will not stay local. Techniques that are developed against one system will meet its commercial relatives elsewhere, which is an argument for designs based on principles rather than on tricks for one country.

One recent episode illustrates how network control reaches the naming layer. On 28 October 2026, Iran’s cybersecurity authority Afta urged organizations to migrate from foreign domains to .ir, citing the risk of sanctions-driven domain suspension. This shifts the threat model. For a platform hosted abroad on a foreign domain, the state’s main lever is blocking at the network level, and the site may remain reachable through circumvention. A domain under a domestic registry, by contrast, places namespace-level control with the state.

Two further details from the 2026 shutdowns matter for what follows. First, circumvention was itself targeted. Chatham House reports that Starlink use is criminalized, with penalties of up to two years, and that the state reportedly uses jamming. Second, the shutdown decision was described as a security-institution decision: Iran International quoted a government spokesperson saying that security policymakers had decided the national network had to be cut and that the government could not override that decision. For design purposes, this means the people operating in-country infrastructure are a compliance point, and a design that depends on their cooperation is fragile.

Existing tools such as Tor with Snowflake, Psiphon, Lantern, and a long list of VPN protocols have done real work. This section is not a critique of them. It is a catalogue of the pressures that no single tool handles well.

A circumvention method that works on one ISP today may fail on another, and may fail on the first tomorrow. There is evidence at several levels:

A design that treats the censor as a single adversary will be wrong on at least some networks. Each ISP should be treated as an independent adversary.

When only approved destinations are reachable, one tactic is to tunnel through approved IP ranges. Community reports on the net4people forum describe exactly this in Russia, and also describe a crackdown in January 2026 in which Roskomnadzor reportedly demanded that cloud providers separate the address pools used for whitelisting from those used for other customers. In March and April 2026, as noted above, whitelisted platforms were told to block VPN users. A related failure mode is worth naming: in Iran, circumvention developers reported a "no-ping" pattern in which a VPN shows as connected but cannot pass data (see the FilterWatch report above). A tool that only checks whether a handshake succeeded will mislead its user. The pattern is the allowlist era's version of the old arms race: every trick that rides on collateral dependency invites a countermeasure that raises the cost of that dependency.

Russia's arms race is not one-sided in tooling. TechRadar, citing Forbes Russia, reports that Roskomnadzor was set to allocate about 2.27 billion rubles to build an AI-powered traffic-filtering mechanism aimed at prohibited content and VPN connections. This is a secondary report and should be treated with care, but the direction is plausible: classification is a natural fit for machine learning, and any circumvention approach should assume it.

Direct-to-satellite connectivity avoids the national network, but Chatham House reports that its use is criminalized in Iran and that jamming has been reported. It is a valuable tool but not a universal answer.

Mesh messengers deserve a short note. The Electronic Frontier Foundation's guide to circumventing shutdowns says apps such as Briar are hard for most people to use and rarely installed, while Bitchat saw some success in Iran. A Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute report notes the claimed range of around 300 meters, which fits dense gatherings rather than cities, and calls the technology immature. Mesh does answer a real need in a total shutdown, but it requires nearby participants, preinstallation, and some technical comfort. For the average user, that is a high bar.

It is tempting to say that blockchain naming and content-addressed storage (ENS, IPFS) solve the namespace-control problem. They help in principle, since no registry can seize a name that no registry owns. In practice, three problems appear:

The conclusion for design is that web3 components should be invisible to the end user. They can help operators coordinate, but they cannot be the thing the user has to understand.

Putting this together, a modern circumvention system must cope with:

Before proposing anything, it is worth stating what the literature supports. These are the design principles the rest of the article leans on.

Diversity beats mimicry. The GFW findings above show that being random is itself detectable, and the parrot-style approach of imitating another protocol tends to fail when imitation is imperfect. The robust alternative is not one clever disguise but many options, chosen according to what works.

Cheap, ephemeral endpoints. Snowflake uses temporary WebRTC proxies run by volunteers, which makes it hard to enumerate and block by address, since proxies come and go.

Hide in collateral, carefully. Conjure uses unused address space belonging to cooperating ISPs (refraction networking), so that a censor who wants to block proxies has to block address space that might hold legitimate services.

Automate strategy discovery. Geneva uses a genetic algorithm to evolve packet-manipulation strategies, and it discovered strategies effective against censors in China, India, and Kazakhstan. A follow-up, Come as You Are, found strategies applied only on the server side, helping unmodified clients, and tested against censors including Iran's at the time. These results are from 2019 and 2020 and say nothing definitive about today's systems, but they establish that strategy search can be automated and that evasion does not have to be client-only.

Distribute access with care. Lox is a bridge distribution system that combines trust levels, invitations, open entry for new users, and anonymous credentials so that the social graph of inviters stays private. Its design goal is that a censor cannot enumerate bridges just by joining. The authors also identify a scaling concern: the cost of the blockage-check protocol grows with the number of blocked bridges, which a patient censor could exploit to disrupt migrations during a critical event. Note that Lox, as published, relies on a single central authority that issues and verifies credentials, and the authors present it as a proof of concept with demonstrative parameters.

Censors have limits. As shown in Section 3.2, inspection costs compute. This is a design observation, not an attack recommendation.

Many readers will be thinking: if strategy search can be automated, why not let AI agents manage the whole thing? There is real momentum behind that idea in enterprise networks. A Cisco and Omdia survey of 1,000 IT and network operations leaders found 84% expect an AI-led operating model within 12 months, though 56% still prefer a human to approve actions before an AI takes them and 24% favor full autonomy.

But agents bring a cost that matters here. Cisco's 2026 report AI Impact on Wide Area Networks, summarized by SDxCentral, finds that an AI agent generates about 450 percent more traffic for a task than a human doing the same task, with roughly 70 percent of that traffic being inference. The report projects enterprise traffic growing about nine-fold by 2035 with widespread agent adoption, compared with about 2.5-fold without, and AI inference reaching about a quarter of total traffic.

Two cautions apply. These are vendor-produced figures for enterprise WANs, and an analyst commentary notes that the headline multiplier is not a general estimate for all agent tasks. And the traffic cited is mostly agents talking to models, not agents configuring networks. Still, the direction of the lesson is clear and it transfers to censored networks, where it bites harder:

This gives a set of design rules that the next section follows:

This section describes a hypothesis, not a tested system. It assembles known components into an architecture aimed at the pressures in Section 5.

Architecture overview: a local agent, VPN app, transport pool and anonymous credential on the user's device; sticky relay shards on the operator side; and a thin coordination layer with an on-chain registry and a findings ledger. The data path never touches the chain.

The agent is a small program on the user's device. Its job is not to carry traffic, only to decide how to try. It is event-driven rather than always running (Section 8.9).

Where does AI actually help here? Honestly, a lot of the selection problem can be handled with classic online learning. The places where learned models earn their keep are:

A back-of-envelope illustration of the control-plane budget (assumptions, not measurements): if the network tracks 50 transports across 20 coarse network classes with a 2-bit success bucket for each, a full status summary is 50 × 20 × 2 bits = 2,000 bits, or about 250 bytes. Even with metadata, that is orders of magnitude smaller than a single inference call. The point is to make the budget explicit and then enforce it.

The heart of the proposal is how users get relays. Two meanings of "sharding" are in play, and it is worth keeping them apart:

An earlier version of this sketch re-assigned every client to a fresh shard each epoch. A toy simulation (Section 8.10) showed why that is a mistake: re-randomizing lets even a few quiet infiltrators see new relays every epoch and enumerate the whole pool over time. Persistent shards cap what any one identity can ever learn.

A blockchain does not belong in the data path. Latency, cost, and transparency all count against it. What it can do well is small, slow-moving coordination:

Critically, users never interact with the chain. They see an app that connects. The earlier-discussed usability problem with wallets and naming is avoided by design. This also forces honest answers to hard questions:

Blockchain sharding has real deployments and also real lessons.

What transfers is the idea of partitioning to limit blast radius and parallelize load. What does not transfer is cross-shard consensus machinery, which this design avoids by keeping data paths off-chain and shard membership soft. The known cost of sharding, that smaller groups are easier to attack, appears here as the infiltration problem described above, and it should be stated plainly.

When preferred paths fail, the agent walks down a ladder rather than failing outright:

Mesh and satellite appear only as complements, outside this design's scope.

A user on ISP A can connect on Tuesday through one transport. On Wednesday, a block lands. The local agent sees repeated resets, classifies them as probable injection, and tries alternatives from its pool, using a few kilobytes at most. Meanwhile the same user's cousin on ISP B, where the block never appeared, keeps using the original. Neither user does anything technical, and neither sees a wallet. Both keep their shard until it is blocked. A censor operating a fake client sees only the relays in its own shard, and each identity it adds must earn trust slowly, so infiltration cannot scale quickly.

None of this has been tested in the field. The scenario shows the intended behavior, not a result.

The agent does not have to be a VPN. It can be a separate layer whose only product is a ranked list of paths that currently work on the user’s network, handed to a tunnel app that does the actual connecting. This is not a new pattern: the Outline SDK’s Smart Dialer already searches a configured set of strategies for one that unblocks DNS and TLS for a list of test domains, and its documentation notes that obtaining a Psiphon config may require a contract with the Psiphon team. The proposal here extends the idea with shared, sharded intelligence about what works where.

Two ways to ship it. The reference experience is the agent as a module inside the project's own VPN app. Third-party VPN apps can integrate the same layer through an API or SDK under agreed terms (the contractual and legal side is out of scope here). In both cases the interface is narrow: the agent returns ranked paths with parameters and a time-to-live, the VPN app connects, and the VPN app reports only success, failure, and coarse timing. The agent never sees user traffic.

An event-driven lifecycle, not continuous monitoring.

This keeps control-plane cost bursty and small, and it avoids a measurement problem: on Android, only one VPN connection can be active at a time, and probes sent while a tunnel is up would measure the tunnel rather than the underlying path. Measuring only when no tunnel is active sidesteps that. It does not shrink the data plane: carrying user traffic remains the VPN's job and cost. Platform limits matter, too. Android exposes network and VPN state changes to apps, while iOS gives far less background freedom, so on iOS the logic would likely live inside the VPN app's own lifecycle rather than a separate always-on app.

Guided discovery, not blind scanning. The agent should find new open paths by exploring a structured search space (fronting combinations, transport parameters, new relay candidates from its shard) with a per-run probe budget. Sweeping arbitrary third-party address space from a phone would be slow, noisy, and easy for a censor to flag.

Candidate confidentiality. Candidate lists can be distributed encrypted under per-epoch keys, with a memory-hard key-derivation step or a time-lock-style puzzle so that bulk decryption is costly. This hides lists at rest and in transit and raises the price of mass enumeration. It is not access control: a censor running a copy of the agent holds the same decryption capability as a real one, and a datacenter has far more compute than a mid-range phone. The real gate remains the trust-level credential from Section 8.4.

A shared findings ledger. Agents with credentials can sign reports of what worked on which network class. A permissioned ledger (for example, proof-of-authority, run by validators from diverse jurisdictions) can serve as an append-only log: commitments and small summaries on-chain, bulk data off-chain. A candidate is promoted only after confirmation by several independent agents from different network classes, and old confirmations decay. Two cautions apply. A small validator set is a coercion and seizure target, and a signed but malicious agent can still try to poison the log. If a chain is more than the problem needs, a Merkle-tree transparency log with signed gossip is the minimal alternative.

Permanent anchoring. One place where permanent storage fits is as a public anchor for the ledger's history. Arweave asks uploaders for a one-time, upfront contribution to a storage endowment, priced to cover roughly 200 years of replicated storage at present prices (Arweave documentation). A signed checkpoint of the ledger (a Merkle root plus validator signatures, a few kilobytes per day) can be written there by an operator outside the censored region, and the one-time fee for something that small should be modest; check the current price before relying on that. This does not stop validators from being coerced, but it makes silent rewriting of history detectable, and it gives researchers a durable archive of aggregated, anonymized results. It must not hold relay addresses, per-user reports, or credentials: data that can never be deleted would become a permanent enumeration list and a permanent record of who reported what. Nor is it a bootstrap path, since reads go through HTTP gateways that can be blocked like any other, so clients should fetch it through the tunnel.

To check the central claims, I wrote two small simulations (code and results). They simulate a simplified model with assumed parameters. They are not measurements of any real network, and the numbers should be read as how the toy behaves, not as predictions.

Per-ISP transport selection. Six simulated ISPs block 12 transports independently and change over time. Averaged over 12 seeds, a client with one fixed transport failed to connect about 61 percent of the time. Random failover failed 7.6 percent and needed about 2.3 tries per connection. A single global ranking failed 2.6 percent. A per-ISP local agent failed 1.2 percent with 1.5 tries, and a per-ISP agent that also used pooled reports from other users on the same ISP (with a one-day lag) connected on the first try about 90 percent of the time. This assumes the pooled reports are honest; poisoning is not modelled.

Relay distribution under infiltration. The simulated censor creates fake identities, learns whatever relays they are given, and blocks them, either immediately ("naive") or after staying quiet and then striking at once ("patient").

Sticky shards + eviction of repeat offenders

The sentence to design toward is: "It works like a VPN app." If the user has to understand epochs, shards, bonds, or keys, the design has failed, because the lesson of mesh networking and wallet-based naming is that technical-user-only tools do not spread.

If this direction interests you, these are the questions where progress would matter most:

Whether the answer is hardware, software, or a mix, the design principle is the same: no single path is permanent, so resilience has to come from diversity, adaptation, and a control plane small enough to survive the conditions it is trying to beat.

#9726. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9725. The Silicon-Carbon Battery Breakthrough Behind 7,000mAh Smartphones

Founder of GadgetGyaan (thegadgetgyaan.com). Plain-English buying guides and explainers on phones, laptops and gadgets.

Founder of GadgetGyaan (thegadgetgyaan.com). Plain-English buying guides and explainers on phones, laptops and gadgets.

Founder of GadgetGyaan (thegadgetgyaan.com). Plain-English buying guides and explainers on phones, laptops and gadgets.

For almost five years, phone batteries were stuck. Flagships from Apple, Samsung, and Google hovered around 4,500 to 5,000mAh, and "two-day battery life" was something only chunky gaming phones could promise. Then, in about 18 months, everything changed. The OnePlus 15 ships with 7,300mAh. Tecno has put 8,000mAh into a phone that is 7.42mm thick. Honor sells a phone with a 10,000mAh battery that is 8.3mm thick.

None of this came from making phones bigger. It came from changing one material inside the battery. Here is what silicon-carbon batteries are, why they work, what they cost you, and why the iPhone and Galaxy in your pocket probably still don't have one.

Every lithium-ion battery has two electrodes. When you charge your phone, lithium ions move from the cathode into the anode and are stored there. When you use your phone, they move back, and that flow powers the device.

For decades, the anode has been made of graphite. Graphite is cheap, stable, and predictable, but it has a hard limit: it can hold one lithium ion for every six carbon atoms. Once the industry had squeezed out almost all the efficiency it could from graphite, the only way to add capacity was to make the battery physically bigger.

Silicon changes the maths. Per gram, silicon can in theory store 4 to 10 times as much lithium as graphite, according to LG Energy Solution. Even a small amount of silicon in the anode raises how much energy fits in the same space.

That is what a "silicon-carbon" battery is: a normal lithium-ion battery whose anode mixes silicon into a carbon structure instead of using graphite alone. The cathode, the electrolyte, and the way you charge it stay basically the same.

Because silicon swells. When it absorbs lithium, it can expand to several times its original volume: by up to 300% when fully charged, according to Android Authority. A phone battery that grew like that would crack its own electrodes within a few charges, and it would push against the screen and the back of the phone.

Manufacturers manage this in three main ways:

The result is a battery that is denser than graphite but still behaves well enough to survive years of daily charging.

Estimates vary: Android Authority puts the gain at roughly 10 to 20% more capacity in the same space, while How-To Geek cites 20 to 50%. In practice, that is roughly the difference between a 5,500mAh battery and a 7,000mAh battery without making the phone any thicker.

Phone makers have spent that extra capacity in two ways:

Some brands have pushed the first approach to the extreme. Honor's 10,000mAh phone and Tecno's 7.42mm, 8,000mAh phone would have been impossible with graphite anodes a few years ago.

Silicon-carbon batteries are a real improvement, but they are not free.

They may wear faster. Even with all the engineering above, silicon still expands and contracts on every charge. Over hundreds of cycles, that stress adds up. A battery engineer interviewed on the Waveform podcast said these batteries tend to lose more capacity in their first two to three years than conventional cells, according to 9to5Google. Brands make strong claims of their own: OnePlus, for example, says the OnePlus 15 battery keeps 80% of its capacity after four years, based on its own simulated tests. Independent long-term data is still limited, because most of these phones are less than two years old.

Some capacity may be held back. To slow wear, makers can limit how much of the battery is used. Nothing is a clear example: the Nothing Phone (3) has a silicon-carbon cell with a physical capacity of 5,500mAh, but outside India it is sold as a 5,150mAh phone, according to 9to5Google.

They are harder to make at scale. Silicon anodes rely on complex nanotechnology processes that currently cost more than making graphite, according to How-To Geek.

This is the part that surprises most people. The biggest obstacle is not chemistry. It is shipping rules.

International transport regulations treat lithium-ion batteries as dangerous goods. Under UN Special Provision 188, which air, sea and road regulators (including the US rules in 49 CFR) all follow, a cell of up to 20 watt-hours can ship under simplified rules. Above that, the device needs dangerous-goods handling, labelling and paperwork. At a typical 3.8 volts, 20Wh works out to roughly 5,300mAh.

Look at Western flagships with that number in mind. The Galaxy S25 Ultra's 5,000mAh battery is about 19.4Wh, and the Pixel 9 Pro's 5,060mAh battery is about 19.7Wh, according to 9to5Google. They sit just under the line.

Apple, Samsung and Google ship hundreds of millions of phones, mostly through global supply chains. For them, a battery that changes their shipping status or needs a two-cell design is a big logistics and cost decision. Samsung also has a long memory: after the Galaxy Note 7 battery recall in 2016, it has tended to adopt new battery technology slowly and carefully. Samsung is rumored to be testing a dual-cell battery design, but so far the big brands have chosen proven graphite cells and longer software support over headline capacity.

What this means if you are buying a phone

Silicon-carbon is not the end point. Battery makers are steadily increasing the share of silicon in anodes, and brands are already testing 10,000mAh cells in normal-size phones. The open questions are the same ones that held the big brands back: how these batteries age over four or five years, how they handle heat during fast charging, and whether shipping rules will change.

For now, the result is simple. If you want the longest battery life in a normal-size phone, the brands using silicon-carbon cells are ahead, and the gap is the biggest it has been in years.

Founder of GadgetGyaan (thegadgetgyaan.com). Plain-English buying guides and explainers on phones, laptops and gadgets.

#9724. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9723. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!
