#9710. Jam Unggah Malam vs Siang di Threads: Benarkah Likes-nya Beda?

description: Aku membandingkan likes 40 unggahan Threads di jam makan siang dan jam santai malam. Hasilnya mengajarkan satu hal penting soal data yang miring.

Ada anggapan yang sering kita dengar: unggah di malam hari, soalnya orang lagi santai dan lebih banyak yang scroll. Aku penasaran apakah anggapan itu bisa dibuktikan dengan angka, jadi aku jadikan bahan tugas statistika.

Pertanyaannya sederhana: apakah unggahan Threads yang naik di jam 19.00-20.59 WIB mendapat likes lebih banyak daripada yang naik di jam 12.00-13.59 WIB?

Jawabannya ternyata tidak sesederhana "malam menang". Sepanjang jalan, aku ketemu hampir semua topik dasar statistika: rata-rata, peluang, Z-score, distribusi normal, dan interval kepercayaan. Artikel ini merangkum semuanya, plus kode Python-nya.

Populasinya adalah semua unggahan publik Threads dengan kata kunci tertentu (kerja, kopi, makan, macet). Jelas aku tidak bisa menghitung semuanya, jadi aku ambil sampel.

Aku mengumpulkan 244 kandidat dari hasil pencarian, lalu menyaringnya dengan aturan yang tidak melihat jumlah likes sama sekali:

Hasil akhirnya 40 unggahan: 20 siang dan 20 malam.

Ada dua catatan jujur soal bias. Pertama, unggahan yang muncul di pencarian sudah disaring algoritma, jadi ini bukan sampel acak murni. Kedua, jumlah followers tidak aku kendalikan, padahal itu pengaruh besar ke likes. Dua hal ini jadi keterbatasan yang harus kubawa sampai kesimpulan.

Angka pertama yang kulihat langsung bikin senang:

Malam menang dua kali lipat, kan? Tunggu dulu. Perhatikan betapa jauhnya mean dari median.

Bayangkan sebuah warung kopi. Sebagian besar pelanggan menghabiskan Rp20.000, lalu suatu hari datang satu orang yang memborong Rp5 juta untuk acara kantor. Rata-rata pengeluaran hari itu melonjak, padahal pelanggan "biasa" tidak berubah sama sekali. Median (nilai tengah) tidak terpengaruh oleh si pemborong, jadi ia lebih jujur menggambarkan pelanggan yang umum.

Data likes persis begitu. Ada satu unggahan siang yang tembus 19.100 likes dan satu unggahan malam dengan 43.400 likes, sementara unggahan paling sepi cuma 2 dan 4 likes. Satu lagi: tidak ada nilai likes yang kembar, jadi modusnya tidak ada. Tidak perlu dipaksa mencari modus kalau memang tidak ada.

Kalau semua titik digambar satu per satu (pakai skala log supaya 2 likes dan 43.400 likes sama-sama terlihat), tampak jelas bahwa kedua kelompok sebarannya lebar dan saling menimpa.

Di Python, bagian ini cuma beberapa baris:

Nilai skewness-nya 2,65 (siang) dan 3,13 (malam). Angka sebesar itu artinya data miring tajam ke kanan.

Pertanyaan berikutnya: kalau sebuah unggahan naik malam hari, berapa peluangnya dapat lebih dari 50 likes?

Rumusnya P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). Dari data, 18 dari 20 unggahan malam punya likes di atas 50, jadi:

Lalu kuhitung hal yang sama untuk siang: ternyata juga 0,90. Peluang keseluruhan (36 dari 40) pun 0,90.

Karena P(>50 | malam) sama dengan P(>50) secara umum, kedua kejadian ini independen: tahu bahwa unggahan naik malam tidak mengubah peluang lolos 50 likes. Analoginya seperti melempar koin dan hujan turun. Hasil lemparan koin tidak berubah hanya karena di luar sedang hujan.

Satu detail kecil: ada satu unggahan siang yang likes-nya tepat 50. Karena soalnya "lebih dari 50", unggahan itu tidak dihitung. Hal-hal sepele seperti ini sering menggeser angka kalau tidak dicatat.

Z-score mengukur seberapa jauh sebuah nilai dari rata-rata, dihitung dalam satuan simpangan baku:

Analogi gampangnya tinggi badan. Kalau rata-rata tinggi di kelas 165 cm dan simpangan bakunya 6 cm, siswa setinggi 183 cm punya Z = 3. Dia bukan sekadar tinggi, dia benar-benar mencolok.

Untuk unggahan terviral, Z-score-nya 3,66 (siang) dan 3,88 (malam). Hampir semua data normal berada di antara Z = -3 dan 3, jadi dua unggahan itu pencilan yang sangat ekstrem.

Nah, di sini aku sempat tersandung. Menghitung peluang dengan distribusi normal mengasumsikan data berbentuk lonceng simetris. Uji Shapiro-Wilk bilang data likes mentahku jelas tidak normal (p < 0,001). Bukti paling lucunya: kalau tetap dipaksa pakai model normal pada data siang, model itu memperkirakan sekitar 28% peluang unggahan punya likes negatif. Padahal likes negatif tidak ada.

Solusinya transformasi logaritma. Setelah np.log(likes), bentuk datanya jauh lebih mendekati lonceng, dan uji normalitasnya lolos (p = 0,48 untuk siang dan 0,24 untuk malam).

Sebagai contoh, peluang unggahan malam punya likes antara 1.000 dan 5.000 versi normal mentah adalah 15,7%, versi log-normal 26,8%, sementara data nyatanya 10%. Dengan sampel sekecil ini, tidak ada model yang pas sempurna, tapi versi log setidaknya tidak menghasilkan peluang yang mustahil.

Mean sampel (2.570 dan 5.390) cuma tebakan titik untuk rata-rata populasi. Interval kepercayaan memberi rentang tebakannya. Analoginya menebak berat badan teman: "sekitar 60 kg" itu estimasi titik, sedangkan "antara 57 dan 63 kg, aku cukup yakin" itu interval.

Karena n hanya 20 per kelompok, aku pakai distribusi t (bukan Z 1,96):

Kedua interval sangat lebar dan saling tumpang tindih. Kalau dihitung dengan rata-rata geometrik (versi log, lebih cocok untuk data miring), polanya sama: siang 502 (176 sampai 1.431), malam 1.184 (412 sampai 3.405).

Secara angka, malam memang lebih tinggi. Tapi sebagai bonus, aku jalankan uji Welch dan Mann-Whitney, dan keduanya menolak untuk memihak (p = 0,25 dan 0,17, jauh di atas 0,05). Artinya selisih yang kulihat masih bisa terjadi hanya karena kebetulan, apalagi dengan sebaran selebar ini.

Kesimpulan yang bisa dipertanggungjawabkan: data ini belum cukup membuktikan bahwa jam unggah memengaruhi likes. Sepertinya faktor lain, seperti isi unggahan, jumlah followers, dan apakah ada yang ikut membagikan, jauh lebih menentukan daripada jamnya.

Semua kode lengkap (termasuk pembuatan keenam chart) ada di repositori ini: SOURCE CODE. Kalau kamu menemukan celah di metodeku, tulis di kolom komentar. Aku senang dikoreksi.

Disclaimer Penggunaan AI: Pengolahan awal data mentah dan penulisan kode analisis statistik pada tulisan ini menggunakan asistensi Claude Sonnet 5.5. Penulis bertanggung jawab penuh atas verifikasi kode, akurasi output statistik, dan interpretasi akhir dari seluruh data yang disajikan.

#9709. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9708. SQL Self-Join Explained with the Simplest Example

A self-join is when you join a table to itself. The first time you see it, you might think "wait, JOIN the same table…?", but ⭐️ it's the go-to technique when parent-child or boss-subordinate relationships live in a single table.

Bosses are also employees, so they're in the same employees table.

When you want to "list each employee alongside their boss's name", you join employees again under a different alias.

Since it's the same table, the trick is to give it aliases like AS emp / AS boss and treat them as separate tables.

Without aliases, there's no way to tell "which name?"

We want to keep people with no boss (like the department head) in the result, so we use LEFT JOIN. With INNER JOIN, the rows without a boss would disappear.

When parent-child or boss-subordinate relationships are in the same table, joining the table to itself under an alias lets you put "the row + its related row" on one line. That's a self-join.

It shines in designs that keep "relationships between things of the same kind" in one table: employee × boss, category × parent category, company × its parent company, and so on.

#9707. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9706. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9705. OPT Came Through After a Long Wait Abroad. Why a School May Refuse a Travel Signature Past Five Months

This is not legal advice. It is general information only, and ByteBridge Talent LLC is not a law office. If this situation is yours, talk with your DSO and a licensed immigration attorney before you make a travel plan. The DSO is the Designated School Official at your international office.

A public discussion this month described a bind that is easy to walk into. A student finished a degree, filed for post-completion Optional Practical Training (OPT). Then the student left the United States to wait for the card, because staying without work permission was too expensive. The wait stretched to about six months. The card was approved, a job was waiting, and a flight was booked. When the student asked the school for an updated Form I-20 and a travel signature, the school said it could not issue one. The student had been outside the country for more than five months, and could not come back on the current F-1 record.

Replies did not agree. One person thought the school was being too strict and did not know of a legal bar. Another said the five-month rule is firm. That person said a return would take a brand-new I-20 with a new record, which would also mean starting over on OPT. Those are two very different outcomes, so it helps to separate what the official pages actually say from what a given school may decide.

Readmission after a short trip. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(4) describes how an F-1 student may be readmitted after "a temporary absence of five months or less." In that case, the student presents a current I-20 signed by the DSO for reentry, or an updated I-20. If the information on the last form has changed, the student presents an updated I-20. That paragraph is written as a path for absences of five months or less. It does not, in the same words, say what a port officer must do after five months. We do not treat it as a complete answer on its own.

Coming back on OPT. A separate paragraph, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(13)(ii), covers a student who already has an unexpired Employment Authorization Document (EAD) for post-completion practical training. That student "may return to the United States to resume employment after a period of temporary absence," if otherwise admissible. The card must be used with an I-20 that the DSO signed for reentry, and that signature has to be no older than six months. An approved card, by itself, is not the full set of papers this paragraph describes. The paragraph does not give its own five-month limit. How it sits next to (f)(4) is a question for your DSO and an attorney, not for a forum.

The SEVIS termination reason. SEVIS is the government's student record system. The current SEVIS Help Hub page on termination reasons (last updated April 9, 2025) includes a reason called "Absent from Country for Five Months." ICE's fact sheet on the same list (updated May 16, 2025) includes that reason too. A DSO is told to use it when both of these are true. The student is known to be outside the United States, and the student has been outside for five months or longer. The pages do not describe this as an automatic system action. They describe it as a reason a DSO may enter. Whether a particular school will enter it, and when, is the school's decision.

If the record is ended. The Help Hub page on ending a student record (last updated April 30, 2026) lists what a termination for a status violation means. Work permission ends. The person can't return on that record. There's no grace period for a status violation. One way to try to return is a new I-20 for initial attendance, with a new SEVIS number and a fresh I-901 SEVIS fee. That path, the page says, starts the F-1 benefits clock over. Eligibility for practical training often depends on completing one full academic year while in F-1 status, so a restart can affect OPT. That is a legal point to review with an attorney, not a result we can promise or rule out.

An older Study in the States blog post from January 14, 2015, "What is the Five-Month Rule?", describes a similar new-I-20 path. The page itself warns that the content may be outdated. We mention it only so you can see the warning, and we rely on the current regulation and the current Help Hub pages above.

Not legal advice. Official pages and school practice change, so read the links above. For your own facts, get help from your international office and a licensed immigration attorney.

#9704. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

#9703. Bethlehem Clears 65,000-Square-Foot Data Center Development in Pennsylvania

The Bethlehem Planning Commission voted unanimously to approve a two-story, 65,000-square-foot data center planned for an industrial park near Routes 22 and 378, closing out a hearing that drew dozens of residents who came to voice their opposition to the project.

The decision, reached in front of a packed audience, did not quiet the crowd.

*Approval Secured for 120-MW Data Center * During the vote and afterward, opponents expressed their frustration at both commissioners and the development team, at one point shouting "shame" together in unison.

The project, a collaboration between data-center company Tensor IQ and construction contractor Boyle Construction, involves plans to develop a 120-megawatt facility on a vacant parcel at 2184 Industrial Drive. Announced in August, the proposed development adds to the growing pipeline of Data Center Projects in the US, highlighting continued investment in large-scale data center infrastructure.

Approval came in two parts: commissioners first unanimously granted three waivers to the city's land development application requirements, then unanimously granted the project its final approval.

*What the Developers Promised on Noise, Water, and Power * Dylan Panebianco, Vice President of operations at Boyle Construction, addressed both the commission and the crowded hearing room, telling them the data center's plans would mitigate impacts on sound, pollution, and electric bills for the surrounding area. On the power side, the facility will depend on three natural gas generators housed in a basement 20 feet below ground.

Those generators are expected to supply roughly 20% of the data center's energy needs, but they also have the capacity to power the entire facility on their own in the event of power outages or strain on the electrical grid.

Beyond the on-site equipment, the developers committed to financing USD 86 million in upgrades to the electrical grid and to covering the cost of a new natural gas line that will feed the center. Cooling at the facility will be handled by a closed loop system installed on the building's roof, which uses a combination of water and glycol.

The developers said the system will not draw water from local waterways. Even so, the data center is projected to use approximately 45 million gallons of water, a figure tied to Environmental Protection Agency requirements for mitigating pollution from the natural gas generators through evaporation into the air.

Noise was another point the developers emphasized. The facility is expected to generate no more than 55 decibels, a level that falls within the city's legal requirements and sits well below the maximum noise levels already measured in the area, which reach around 70 decibels. Sean Boyle, President of Boyle Construction, framed the proposal as a good fit for its location.

"We think this is the right project in the right site," he said. "We've tried to be conscious about the community, the noise, the sound, as you can see, the water, and the electric.

And we want this to be something that at the end of the day, we can all be proud of."

*Residents Press Their Case and Say Information Was Lacking * The developers' assurances did not satisfy the opponents who filled the room. Residents argued that the development team had not gone far enough to shield neighbors from potential harms and had failed to supply enough detail about what they were planning.

A key point of contention involves Bethlehem's own regulatory timeline. Last month, the city approved an ordinance that tightens restrictions on data centers within city limits.

Because the developers filed their application before that ordinance took effect, the project is not subject to the stricter rules it created.

The developers acknowledged as much, saying their plans meet nearly all of the requirements in the new ordinance, with one notable exception: the "setback" rules, which require data centers to be at least 1,000 feet from "sensitive" uses such as homes, schools, and hospitals.

Although the proposed facility sits in an industrial area, it would be located just north of a residential neighborhood across Route 22. Bret Becker, who lives in that neighborhood, pressed the commission on what residents would actually gain from the project.

"What will be the true benefit to this community with this? I don't see any. From my standpoint, where I live, there is nothing," he said. "Developers say they're in the local community; that's fine, but on that picture [of the proposed data center site], you could see my house. Do you see your houses there? Would you want your house right next to a data center?"

**Why Commissioners Looked Past the Crowd's Anger **Commission members acknowledged the depth of feeling in the room but explained that their role is narrower than many in the audience hoped. They said they are charged with evaluating land development proposals against the city's laws and regulations, not weighing public opposition itself.

Commission Chair Robert Melosky laid out that reasoning in his remarks. "Bethlehem can welcome responsible private investment while insisting on and putting on those guardrails and insisting on accountability, transparency, and compliance with applicable standards," he said.

"Our job is not to stand in the way of progress; our job is to make certain that progress occurs responsibly and with protections. And I believe that if the applicant has demonstrated he is in compliance." Waivers and a Community Benefits Pledge Folded into the Approval Alongside technical commitments covering power, water, and noise, the developers agreed to allocate a portion of their revenue to community-benefit initiatives. Although specific details have not yet been disclosed, they are working with a University of Notre Dame-based activist to conduct public outreach and develop a community benefits agreement.

These commitments form part of the broader US data center projects development landscape, where community engagement and infrastructure sustainability are increasingly important considerations.The legal foundation for the approval rests partly on zoning.

The Industrial Drive site is zoned for industrial use, and under the city's former ordinance, data centers are permitted there "by-right." Still, the developer sought three waivers from the city's land development application requirements, and commissioners granted all three unanimously. The waivers exempt the developer from tree-planting requirements; the developer will instead pay a "fee in lieu of" planting the required trees and from a limit on the width of driveways leading into the data center.

Opponents had specifically asked commissioners to deny the waivers as a way to stall the project, but the commission declined to do so. Instead, members voted unanimously to grant the waiver requests, then moved directly to the final approval vote that cleared the 65,000-square-foot facility over the objections of the crowd in attendance.

#9701. Shared tokens or a dedicated GPU? A short break-even check in Python

Your LLM feature is live, traffic is climbing, and the inference bill comes in two very different shapes: pay per token, or pay per GPU-hour. At what monthly volume does one beat the other? A short Python script answers it for your own numbers.

Inc42 reported on 27 Oct 2026 that Simplismart raised a $14 Mn Series B led by Dallas Venture Capital, with NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC, Micromax and angels participating, to expand what it describes as "the software layer between AI models and GPU infrastructure". The useful detail for builders: it sells the same inference three ways — shared endpoints billed on token consumption with no minimum fee, dedicated endpoints billed by GPU usage and runtime, and bring-your-own-compute — while neoclouds such as Nava, which raised a $22 Mn Series A in April 2026 to build GPU-as-a-service and bare metal, sell the hourly side of the same decision.

Per-token pricing is linear in usage: cost tracks the tokens you send and receive, and it is zero at zero — a quiet week costs nothing. Dedicated pricing is flat per hour: the meter runs whether the GPU serves requests or sits idle, so a quiet week costs the same as a busy one. Dedicated also carries a capacity ceiling, since one box emits only so many tokens per second, and sizing that box is your job. The real question is therefore not "which is cheaper" but "at what monthly volume does the flat bill undercut the linear one — and can one box actually serve that volume?"

The script takes four inputs: shared per-token prices, the GPU hourly rate, hours per month, and the sustained output throughput you measured on your own setup. Every price is an input pasted from your provider's pricing page.

The printed numbers come from illustrative inputs, not any provider's real prices:

Start on shared endpoints. Where the shared plan has no minimum fee (Simplismart's shared model, per Inc42, does not), the experiment costs only the tokens it burns. Log input and output tokens per day from the first request. Once a month, paste your provider's real prices and your measured throughput into the script and re-run it. Move to dedicated only when the logged volume sits above break-even with headroom for idle hours and growth — not when a spreadsheet full of guessed numbers says it might.

One bill is linear and the other is flat; the script shows where they cross, and your logs show which side you stand on.

#9700. The Page Loads Fine — But Its Headers Are Telling a Different Story

Last month a client's site passed every check I could think of. The pages rendered fast. The design was clean. Lighthouse gave it a green score. Then their security auditor sent back a one-page report that read like a failing grade.

Nothing on the page was broken. The problem was invisible — in the response headers. The site was missing four of the five security headers that browsers actually enforce, its pages were not being cached at all, and the server was happily announcing its exact software version to anyone who asked.

I have checked headers on dozens of sites since, and the pattern repeats. Headers are the part of a response nobody looks at until something goes wrong. Here is what they are, what they control, and the five checks I run on every site now.

Every time a browser requests a page, the server sends two things back: the HTML you see, and a set of headers you do not. Headers are short key-value instructions that travel with the response. They tell the browser how to handle the page, how long to cache it, which resources it may load, and what to do when something looks suspicious.

You can see them in any browser. Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, click a request, and look at the Response Headers section. Most developers have never opened that panel. That is the problem.

The HTML is the visible half of a response. The headers are the operating instructions. A site can look perfect and still be shipping instructions that weaken its security, waste bandwidth, or confuse search engines.

There are dozens of response headers, but five do most of the security work. If you check nothing else, check these.

Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) tells browsers to always use HTTPS for your site, even if a link or bookmark points to the plain HTTP version. Without it, a visitor who types your domain without the scheme can be downgraded to an unencrypted connection on the first request. With it, the browser refuses to make that mistake.

Content-Security-Policy (CSP) controls which scripts, styles, and other resources a page is allowed to load, and from where. It is the strongest defence against cross-site scripting, because even if an attacker injects a script into your page, the browser will refuse to run it if the source is not on your approved list.

X-Content-Type-Options with the value nosniff stops browsers from guessing a file's type. Without it, a browser can decide that a file your server called plain text is actually executable script — and run it. This is how some old MIME-sniffing attacks worked.

X-Frame-Options (or the CSP frame-ancestors directive) stops other sites from embedding your pages in a frame. Without it, your login page can be framed inside an attacker's page in a clickjacking attack, where the visitor clicks something they cannot see.

Referrer-Policy controls how much of your URL leaks to other sites when a visitor clicks an outbound link. A strict policy keeps internal paths and query strings out of the referrer header that other sites receive.

None of these headers changes how a page looks. That is exactly why they get skipped. They are invisible work, and invisible work is the first thing cut under deadline pressure.

Here is the uncomfortable truth about security headers: a site missing all five will work perfectly. Pages load. Users log in. Nothing looks wrong. The protections these headers provide only matter when someone is actively attacking the site, or when an auditor checks.

That is why I now treat a header check as part of every launch checklist, next to the SSL certificate and the sitemap. A missing HSTS header is not a cosmetic issue. It is an open door that only shows itself when someone walks through it.

The same logic applies to the audit findings I see most often. The report does not say "your site is broken". It says "your site is unprotected". Those are different sentences, and the second one is the one that costs a client a contract.

Security is only half the story. The other half is caching, and it is where headers quietly cost real performance.

Cache-Control tells browsers and CDNs how long a response can be reused before checking back with the server. When it is missing, or set far too conservatively, every repeat visit re-downloads content that has not changed. Multiply that by every page, every asset, and every visitor, and the cost adds up.

The fix is not complicated, but it is easy to get wrong in the other direction. Versioned files such as app.3f9a.css can be cached for a year, because the filename changes when the content changes. HTML pages usually need a short lifetime, so updates reach visitors quickly.

The classic mistake is caching HTML for a year and then wondering why visitors keep seeing the old homepage. The other classic mistake is caching nothing at all, and wondering why repeat visits feel slow. Both show up in the headers, and both are visible in a single check.

Some headers do not protect or speed anything up. They just talk too much. The Server header announces the server software and often its exact version. X-Powered-By does the same for the application framework.

Neither header breaks anything. But exact version numbers make it slightly easier for an attacker to match your stack against known vulnerabilities. Most teams strip or generalize these headers as a minor hardening step. It is not the most critical fix on the list, but it is free, and there is no reason to advertise your stack to the whole internet.

There is one more header worth watching for, and it is the one that has cost people search traffic: X-Robots-Tag. When it carries noindex, the page is hidden from search engines — even when the HTML looks completely fine. I have seen a staging configuration leak into production this way, with the header quietly deindexing pages while the team wondered why rankings were falling.

You do not need a terminal or a curl command to do this, although curl works fine. The fastest way is a purpose-built tool: paste the URL, run the check, and read the findings in plain English.

When you run an http header check, you get the full response header list alongside the status code, plus a plain-English reading of what is missing. It flags the five security headers above, a missing Cache-Control, and Server or X-Powered-By values that reveal version details. It does not follow redirects, so you see the response for the exact URL you entered — which matters, because a redirect's headers are not the page's headers.

The check takes seconds. What takes longer is deciding what to do with the findings, which brings me to the part most articles skip: the order in which to fix them.

Not every missing header is equally urgent, and fixing them in the wrong order creates new problems. This is the sequence I follow.

First, set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy. Both are safe to add everywhere. They break nothing and close real gaps. There is no reason to delay them.

Second, add X-Frame-Options or a CSP frame-ancestors directive. Unless your site is designed to be embedded in other pages, framing should be blocked. Check first that no legitimate integration depends on framing — some payment widgets do.

Third, enable HSTS — but only once HTTPS works everywhere on the site, including subdomains you plan to include. Browsers remember HSTS for the whole max-age period, and they will refuse plain HTTP for that entire time. Enabling it while some subdomain still serves HTTP will lock visitors out of that subdomain.

Fourth, roll out Content-Security-Policy gradually. Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only and watch the violation reports for a week. This shows you what the policy would block before it blocks anything. Enforcing a strict CSP on a live site without that step is how you break your own scripts in production.

Finally, fix caching. Set long lifetimes on versioned static assets and short lifetimes on HTML. Then re-check, because caching is set at several layers — the server, the CDN, the application — and one layer can override another.

Beyond the five security headers, there are a few header findings that have saved me real debugging time.

The pattern is always the same: the page looks fine, the headers disagree, and the headers are right. When a site misbehaves in a way the HTML cannot explain, the headers are the next place to look.

The reason headers stay unchecked is that nobody owns them. The developer sets them, the hosting provider overrides some of them, the CDN adds its own, and the application sets a few more. Responsibility is spread across four layers, so no single person ever reads the final result.

That is why a header check belongs in the launch checklist and in the periodic audit. Run it after a server migration, after a CDN change, after a plugin update that touches security settings, and after any incident. It takes under a minute, and the findings are either reassuring or actionable. There is no third outcome.

The page your visitors see is only half the response your server sends. The other half is a set of instructions that decides how secure, how fast, and how visible that page really is. Check it before someone else does — because auditors, attackers, and search engines already are.

If you have ever found a header problem that explained a bug nobody could reproduce, I would like to hear about it. The best checklists come from production incidents, and this one is still growing.

#9699. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.
